💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.
  • Industry observers note that geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized.
  • That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a upcoming $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.

Industry observers note that geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy, says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a upcoming $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.

Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.

In a recent development, “We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai mentioned. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”.

Industry observers note that bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.

In a recent development, instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the manufacturer says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.

The startup right now operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai noted.

To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from upcoming customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.

It has been revealed that once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai noted.

The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures, with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.

Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang’s exit

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1451 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Days after Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from the chipmaker he founded 33 years ago, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress will now face intense questions about what comes next.
  • Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly earnings after the close on Tuesday.
  • Huang resigned Thursday, but Nvidia's legions of customers, partners and investors still rely on the manufacturer to continue shipping large quantities of graphics processing units and AI systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Days after Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from the chipmaker he founded 33 years ago, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress will now face intense questions about what comes next.

Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly earnings after the close on Tuesday. While the company is again expected to show explosive growth as the key infrastructure provider to the artificial intelligence boom, Kress and her team will likely be forced to answer questions on chip sales to China, the risks tied to deals with neoclouds and what comes next under newly introduced leadership.

Huang resigned Thursday, but Nvidia's legions of customers, partners and investors still rely on the manufacturer to continue shipping large quantities of graphics processing units and AI systems. Kress, who has been Nvidia's CFO since 2013, was tapped to lead the company while the board searches for a successor.

Analysts expect Nvidia to report 91% revenue growth to $109.1 billion, according to LSEG, with $2.47 in earnings per share.

In a recent development, kress, alongside Huang, offered a full-year growth forecast suggesting that the firm's historic expansion is poised to continue. They remarked revenue expansion in fiscal 2028 would be roughly 70% in what Kress, on the last earnings call, described as a "supply constrained outlook.".

"What would be good for them to do is reiterate that and confirm that is still intact, if they have the ability," said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kunjan Sobhani.

But Kress has to do far more than just put up numbers. The stock has dropped for six straight weeks, the longest losing streak since 2012, pushing the organization's market cap down by $1.7 trillion.

Here are some key issues Kress has to address:.

Sources indicate that huang's public downfall began in October, when The Latest York Times reported that American intelligence agencies were surveilling a woman named Alice Huang, who was close with the former CEO, believing she was a Chinese intelligence asset. The report alleged that Alice Huang was helping smuggle Nvidia's premium chips into China, violating U.S. export controls.

An Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the report saying, "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.".

Nvidia has also insisted that it gets essentially no data center sales from China, consistent with how it reports sales in its recent Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

But Jensen Huang's romantic ties to Alice Huang, a Megaspeed International executive, raised concerns about Nvidia's actual business in China. A substantial part of Nvidia's sales to Southeast Asia, according to some industry experts, are intended for Chinese companies, either through smuggling the chips to the mainland or by building data centers for Chinese clients in Singapore or Malaysia.

In a statement Sunday, a Megaspeed representative noted that the cloud provider is conducting a thorough internal investigation, and that Alice Huang left the organization in 2025.

"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," Megaspeed said in the statement.

Culper Research, a short selling research firm that published a note on Nvidia's "China problem" in May, alleges that 20% of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was "driven by China.".

Industry observers note that nvidia has denied any diversion, and said it has no evidence that any such activity has taken place. But that was before last week's scandal.

Sources indicate that investors will be listening closely to what Kress says about the market for Nvidia's AI chips. Some analysts expect the government to pursue newly introduced rules that would force Nvidia to more closely track its customers and how they strategy to use the company's critical technology.

Kress might not be able to say much, as politicians in Washington, D.C., are ramping up investigations of Nvidia and calling executives to testify in front of Congress.

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Rep. Richard Neal. D-Mass., are probing the administration's approvals for Nvidia chip sales to Chinese companies and asked the Commerce Department to save any communications regarding Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Other representatives are asking law enforcement agencies to look into Huang's tryst with the alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Sources indicate that jensen Huang mentioned he would testify in a closed-door meeting with the chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees. The committees are also looking to meet with current Nvidia executives, including Tim Teter, the general counsel.

If government officials are able to prove that Nvidia knew that its Southeast Asian clients like Megaspeed were pass-throughs to Chinese companies, the scandal could grow even deeper.

Recent findings suggest that "The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client?" Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated in an interview with CNBC on Friday. "And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?".

Huang was singular in creating a newly introduced class of companies called neoclouds, which competed with Nvidia's hyperscaler customers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle and SpaceX — by offering Nvidia compute to smaller AI labs and startups.

Last quarter, Huang noted the organization's neocloud business, which it called ACIE, would drive Nvidia's growth going forward.

Recent findings suggest that but Nvidia had a unique relationship to the neoclouds, which are often new or nascent businesses that need upfront capital in order to secure land, power and Nvidia chips. Nvidia has acted as supplier, investor and financier to these companies.

Huang was integral in deciding who got chips first and publicly pushed to expand Nvidia's role in financing major data center infrastructure.

Sources indicate that for example, Huang in August revealed a program on CNBC to help these types of companies as well as frontier labs access financing from six major financial firms. Huang was central to the effort, which has yet to result in a completed deal, and it's unclear whether Kress has the same ability to rally Wall Street, or if she has the enthusiasm to keep using Nvidia's balance sheet to sell more chips.

"Jensen did all of these innovative deals when it comes to supporting, for example, neoclouds, using his relationships, using his balance sheet," said Sobhani, the Bloomberg Intelligence analyst. "Those deals could slow down.".

It has been revealed that jensen Huang built Nvidia and has acted as its sole figurehead. But while he's been key to helping develop the AI market, the demand now is massive regardless of who's in charge. Nvidia's high-end GPUs are essential for training AI models and can be used to serve models in a process called inference.

Many investors have looked at Nvidia's earnings as a proxy for overall AI demand. Huang noted in August that "demand was accelerating." Kress echoed the point, saying, "Incredibly, we are seeing demand acceleration even at our scale.".

Nvidia's board has said it expects Kress to deliver on Nvidia's commitments to shareholders, customers and partners, but investors worry how long that can last. Morgan Stanley analysts cut their estimates for calendar 2027 and 2028 data center sales by about 10% on the Huang news.

Industry observers note that "We feel certain that we are cutting to an overly conservative number," the analysts wrote, noting that it leaves a lot of room for weaker demand. "But faced with some uncertainty and multiple downgrades, we would rather err on the side of being too conservative.".

Nvidia has spent or committed to spend heavily on memory, wafers and other key components for its products.

In its most recent filing, Nvidia remarked it committed to $92 billion in supply and capacity for the rest of this fiscal year, $87 billion in the fiscal year ending January 2028, and $88 billion in the fiscal year ending January 2029.

Kress is well known to investors and has appeared on the tech giant's conference calls for years, but Tuesday's earnings will be different — she's running the show now.

In the past, Kress would read off prepared remarks about the quarter's results and the company's forecast, then turn it over to Huang, who would singlehandedly answer analyst questions, riffing on everything from the company's technology to the broader AI ecosystem.

Kress sent a short note to staff on the day Huang resigned, but Tuesday's earnings will be the first time Nvidia's external audience will hear from her about the CEO transition, the company's search for a successor, upcoming launch events, or how she and the board are trying to maintain Nvidia's culture and technological lead.

#633. After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1455 w)

After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, not all of them die, though.
  • Recent findings suggest that ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

In a recent development, not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

Recent findings suggest that ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

Sources indicate that but the EV market didn’t take off as swiftly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

Industry observers note that the rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a newly introduced round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.).

Recent findings suggest that part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the firm spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he noted that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet major on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have unveiled their own energy storage products.

Sources indicate that many newly introduced grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the tech giant that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

It has been revealed that my recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a firm pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz stated ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said.

Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz noted the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the tech giant. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz noted. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”.

Sources indicate that today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is presently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

Sources indicate that in its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The organization remarked it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”.

Recent findings suggest that ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

It has been revealed that but it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the organization has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

#631. Breaking: Which Steam settings should you change to improve gaming performance?

Breaking: Which Steam settings should you change to improve gaming performance?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, improving your system's gaming performance involves more than swapping components.
  • While it's a reliable gaming storefront with plenty of community tools, those tools can affect weaker machines or customers on slow internet.
  • It has been revealed that steam's in-game overlay is a powerful tool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When in doubt, disable the overlay.

According to recent reports, improving your system's gaming performance involves more than swapping components. Software can affect your frame rate as much as the system's hardware. Multiple overlays and background apps can rapidly ruin your frame rate in any game. Even if you're selective about what you install, tried-and-true apps can slow your device down if you leave them on their default settings. A great example of this is Steam.

While it's a reliable gaming storefront with plenty of community tools, those tools can affect weaker machines or customers on slow internet. By default, Steam starts when your system boots, loads community assets in the background and uses resources to power its in-game overlay. These small features can eat into your FPS and bandwidth, but the good news is you can turn almost all of them off to improve your gaming performance and system stability. The best place to start is Steam's overlay.

It has been revealed that steam's in-game overlay is a powerful tool. It gives you easy access to community guides, friend invites, frame rate limiters and in-game purchases. As useful as that can be, it comes at a cost: stability. Valve's overlay uses few system resources, lowering your FPS by maybe a couple of percentage points at most. However, many gamers can attest to just how buggy some titles are when the in-game overlay is enabled. With the overlay enabled, games might stutter, drop frames, or even crash. Disabling the overlay is generally a good place to start when these complications occur.

It has been revealed that open Steam and click the top-left corner, then select the "Settings" option. From here, go to the "In Game" tab to view all of your options with the in-game overlay. If you're experiencing major concerns with most of your games, we suggest you toggle the "Enable the Steam overlay while in game" option at the very top of the menu. Your system will no longer use resources to run the overlay's background tools or web browser, saving bandwidth and improving overall system stability.

Industry observers note that if disabling the overlay didn't fix the issue, Steam has a few performance settings you can toggle that should noticeably affect your FPS and bandwidth on weaker hardware. From the same settings menu, head to the "Library" section. There are two settings here that can help: Low Bandwidth Mode and Low Performance Mode. If you are having complications with graphical performance in general, we recommend enabling both and testing your in-game FPS. Should your frame rate improve, try disabling Low Bandwidth Mode and test again.

Sources indicate that low Bandwidth Mode disables Steam's background loading of community assets — community guides, artwork and video content. While this doesn't affect FPS directly, Steam can use a surprising amount of background bandwidth when this setting is disabled. For video games with online components or always-online requirements, leaving this setting on can improve your game's stability and frame rate.

It has been revealed that the other setting, Low Performance Mode, disables some of the advanced graphic effects you'll find in Steam's library tab. It disables category transitions, game selection, and various icons to save system memory. This frees up system resources for whatever game you're playing, though it won't make a night-and-day difference on most systems. Pair this with disabling the in-game overlay to maximize your FPS.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one.
  • To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints.
  • Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a upcoming Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or a handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?

To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a upcoming Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID. I've also removed a couple of discontinued feeders and updated links and prices.

It has been revealed that this cheery blue- or yellow-roofed feeder, from security firm Netvue, was the first smart feeder WIRED tested, back in 2022, when it earned a 6/10 rating due to its high price and wonky AI. Both metrics have improved dramatically since then—Birdfy's app is now the second-most user-friendly on the market, behind only Birdbuddy's, and this feeder is often on sale for around $130. Its AI identification, which is decent, used to be paywalled but is now free with every tier of feeder.

The 1080p/2K camera isn't the best quality you'll find, but it does have one of the widest viewing angles of any smart feeder, at 155 degrees, so you're more likely to get full bird shots, as opposed to just heads and butts. The plastic housing (available in blue or yellow) also makes this feeder durable and easy to clean, and the 50-ounce seed reservoir is super easy to fill with its convenient flip-up top. Not all bundles come with a solar panel, but you can buy one separately. Unlike with other feeders, the solar panel is not built in and needs to be mounted and connected separately with the included 9.8-foot charging cable.

It's not the fanciest feeder on the market, nor the one with the best camera, but I've never had a problem with the two models I've been rotating in and out throughout the years, and the reliability and price point make it the best bet for most backyard birders.

Target (Solar + Extended Perch).

Birdbuddy's brand-new Nook model is a lot of bird feeder for the price; it won our recent head-to-head test of sub-$100 smart feeders. The base $99 model doesn't come with a solar roof or extended perch, as seen in the photo above, but you will get a 2K HDR camera that can shoot vertically or horizontally (it pops in and out via a magnet), as well as the same sturdy, high-quality construction as Birdbuddy's pricier Home model. The seed capacity isn't the greatest at 0.9 liters, but the app is easy to use and can even identify birds nearby that don't land on the feeder, so long as its excellent onboard microphone hears their sounds.

It has been revealed that birdbuddy's Achilles’ heel has always been its sensor, which is slow to wake up and regularly misses bird visits. The fresh Birdbuddy feeder supposedly has a faster wake-up time than previous models, and though it still lagged behind Birdfy's competing Rookie feeder in capturing all visits, the Nook's rate was substantially better than the Home's. It also has more mounting options, allowing for hanging in addition to wall and pole mounts (though the latter is a loose fit), and allows for no-cost manual AI ID of all visitors.

Sources indicate that camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, one of the first to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands, and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The revision has built-in solar panels, an option for pole-mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. The default media type it saves is video, though this is 4K Ultra HD, and the images are—as expected—extremely sharp. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days; however, the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 per year or $4 per month).

According to recent reports, I appreciate the generous 1.5-liter seed hopper, although this, combined with the solar panel and battery, makes it extremely heavy. When filled, it tips the scales at 5 pounds, meaning that if you do pole-mount it, you will need to use both included hose clamps and wrench them tightly. I also wouldn't attempt to mount it on anything unstable, like a wobbly fence. Other original Hibird features that made it to the Pro include the little handles on the assembly screws (so you won't need any assembly tools) and the chunky plastic body. The latter was subjected to a little bit of squirrel-chewing during my test, but it still held up well.

The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is one of the most thoughtfully designed feeders on the market. You don't have to take down the whole feeder when refilling, as the 1.5-liter dual-hopper plastic seed reservoir is removable from the body. The 8-megapixel photos and 4K HD video have much better quality than you'll find from most competitors, and the components come apart for easy cleaning. I also tested the original version, which features a separate solar panel, and my only complaint was that the panel stopped charging the camera after about six weeks. This version features a built-in solar roof, which did an excellent job keeping the feeder charged during its six-week-long test, even on cloudy days. The plastic body is extremely thick and sturdy, and unlike lighter-weight feeders like Birdfy's, it's designed to hold up in more extreme weather.

In a recent development, the app is easy to navigate, and the whole setup is functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription ($90/year, purchasable online or through the Kiwibit app) but you'll be losing out on a lot of features, including 60-day storage and the ability to record up to three minutes of video if a bird is doing something interesting—a unique feature among smart feeders, and one I discovered that I love. (There's nothing more frustrating than having a video cut off right as a bird is about to do something funny.) This smart feeder costs a bit much for what it is, but if you know you like having a smart feeder, I think it's worth the investment. Note, however, that it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, and the warranty is half the length you get from many competitors. I also tested Kiwibit's newer model, the Feeder 2 Pro, and while its camera does have an interesting auto-zoom lens, I didn't think it was worth the $120 premium over this model.

It has been revealed that birdbuddy is known for its user-friendliness and thoughtful app—its Pro Smart Hummingbird Feeder is no exception. The feeder is intuitive and easy to use, and you don't need a subscription to access fun features like AI identification, 5 MP photos, and 2K HD video with slo-mo. A subscription unlocks features like family sharing and a higher bit rate, but the feeder is perfectly functional without those. With the panel being built into the feeder's roof, there’s also no auxiliary solar panel to worry about. Pairing with your phone is a cinch, integrating it into the Birdbuddy app with other feeders is a snap, and even refilling it is no problem. Unlike other hummingbird feeders that have weirdly cavernous capacities and/or need to be filled upside down, the Birdbuddy’s bottom screws off and holds a reasonable 1.75 cups of liquid. This detail is crucial; as the Cornell Lab of Ornithology points out, the easier it is to clean a hummingbird feeder, the more likely you are to do it often and well.

Industry observers note that this feeder also comes with extra plastic flowers and a little brush for scrubbing them, and the app sends reminders when it's time to clean. You'll find fun, seasonal touches in the app, like the ability to send digital bird holiday cards with the photos your feeder captures, and a tool that superimposes hats, clothes, and various accessories on the birds, which is actually funnier than it sounds. However, as with the Birdbuddy seed feeders, the significant downside is that the feeder's sensor doesn’t always pick up every bird that visits. This can definitely be a bummer, particularly when you see something interesting out the window but it doesn’t show up in the app.

After experiencing connection complications with the Birdfy Polygon, I swapped it out for the newer Birdfy Nest Duo and have had no issues. The sleek, contemporary Duo is a fir box fitted with two cameras—one facing the hole and one tucked discreetly inside the feeder. That gives you a full-spectrum view of what's going on. Both cameras have night vision (the internal one is infrared). Like the Polygon, the Duo sports a remote for rebooting and recharging the camera (though the separate solar panel, which can be pole-mounted, has kept the cameras reliably charged), as well as different-size holes for different species, each with its own chew-proof predator guard.

According to recent reports, there's a metal grate with drainage holes that you can slot into grooves in the lower third of the Nest to make the cavity larger or smaller. The interested birds of my yard seemed very put off by the grate, so I covered it with a layer of craft mat moss, which was a success—a chickadee promptly moved in and laid seven eggs, all of which hatched. (I detail the experience in a separate review). For the first time, I was able to use the Birdfy app's ability to collect images from its nest boxes and string them together in a “story” that's shareable online. But I didn't find it especially useful or accurate. No matter, though, because the video captures have been a truly fascinating and educational experience, and I wish I could afford to buy the Duo for everyone I know.

So far, the Duo has been rained on a bunch and survived a couple of heat waves, but the wood finish and black paint are peeling and will need refinishing before I put them up for next season. (The feeder comes equipped with a thermometer and hygrometer to keep an eye on conditions. I recently had to zip-tie an umbrella to mine during a heat wave, which likely saved some fledglings' lives, though the lightweight construction and black-painted side and top probably contributed to the box overheating.).

I rarely expect (or get) compliments on my backyard smart feeders, but I have gotten many on this one, which has a distinctively modern look with natural wood (bamboo that's FSC-certified to be responsibly sourced) and a black-painted side and roof. It blends right into the landscape as opposed to providing a visual pop of plastic. (The pole and baffle shown in the photo above are not included.).

Industry observers note that birdfy's user-friendly app presents 2K HD images and video with free lifetime AI ID, and it's easy to share photos and videos with others. There's a solar panel you can mount separately, but I didn't do this and was impressed that the camera ran for nearly two months on an indoor USB-C charge.

Wood obviously comes with a higher risk of chewing by squirrels and other rodents, but there are metal guards available (both Birdfy-brand and aftermarket) that fit over the seed. I followed the 5-7-9 rule for pole-mounting to avoid this problem, but I was totally shocked at how weathered my feeder got after two months. And this was in a Pacific Northwest dry summer—about as mild as it gets. The finish was completely peeling off, so I recommend adding an extra layer of urethane (this is what I use) before putting it out for the first time, especially now, heading into winter.

Kiwibit’s newly introduced enhancement to its original Feeder 2 is an interesting one; it’s the first bird feeder camera to feature autofocus in 4K HDR. The quality was exceptional, though, during my testing, some birds were alarmed by the camera movement. The biggest downside, though, is that most of this feeder’s features—including AI bird identification, expanded gallery views, and 60-day cloud storage—are now locked behind a $90-a-year paywall. It's not enough of an upgrade to justify paying the extra cash over the base-model Bird Feeder 2.

What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder.

The world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.

Subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features. That's in order to support the company's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it indicates so in the marketing materials or not. You will need to do your due diligence before buying.

It has been revealed that mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole-mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, which is another important detail to confirm before buying.

Recent findings suggest that wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.

Sources indicate that app: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am currently building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.

How Does WIRED Test Bird Feeders?

I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole-mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.

It has been revealed that I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.

The majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the company. I keep some for longer-term testing, put others in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and donate others locally via the Buy Nothing Project.

What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?

Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?

This section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.

It has been revealed that first off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.

According to recent reports, it follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more notable than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.

In a recent development, however, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. A smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.

It has been revealed that as is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.

Industry observers note that the yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.

Sources indicate that another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one from Birdfy. Or you could use seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. The taste doesn't affect birds, since they don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do. That noted, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this, and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

#628. Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (900 w)

Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep.
  • But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy.
  • Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid.

But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep.

Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill.

“Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch.

Sources indicate that speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly.

If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade.

Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup stated it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ F, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital.

Mazama hopes that its upcoming carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market.

Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: A report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies stated that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity.

It has been revealed that geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to 10 times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down.

It has been revealed that accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail.

High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan noted.

Recent findings suggest that instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle and rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit.

“I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he remarked. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super-hot rock temperatures.”.

That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his tech giant hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity.

“What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he stated. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.”.

Hands-on (and off) with Mercedes-Benz's upcoming MB.Drive Assist Pro system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The streets of San Francisco are increasingly littered with oddly shaped cars festooned with bulbous sensors on the outside and no drivers on the inside.
  • According to recent reports, when it comes to cars you can actually own, various manufacturers are making meaningful strides toward autonomy, but all in the form of driver assistance.
  • Next year, Mercedes-Benz is taking its own step forward with advanced driver assistance in the form of Hands-Free Highway Assist and MB.Drive Assist Pro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benz takes us another step towards self-driving.

The streets of San Francisco are increasingly littered with oddly shaped cars festooned with bulbous sensors on the outside and no drivers on the inside. You can't go two minutes without seeing a car from Waymo or Zoox buzz by, proof that the autonomous revolution has hit the Bay Area. Still, those are all limited-use cars, summoned via smartphone, taking you to your destination, then disappearing from your life as quickly as they arrived.

According to recent reports, when it comes to cars you can actually own, various manufacturers are making meaningful strides toward autonomy, but all in the form of driver assistance. These systems do some of the driving some of the time, but under the active supervision of the driver behind the wheel.

Next year, Mercedes-Benz is taking its own step forward with advanced driver assistance in the form of Hands-Free Highway Assist and MB.Drive Assist Pro. To get an early look, I visited that haven of autonomy for some laps of the Bay in the best that Mercedes has to offer.

My first go was behind the wheel of a GLS, Mercedes-Benz's largest and most luxurious SUV. In the high-performance AMG flavor, it's also reasonably fun to drive, but my job for the morning was to sit back and take my hands off the wheel.

Hands-Free Highway Assist is an upcoming feature that will let the driver go hands-free on limited, designated, divided highways. The driver will need to keep paying attention — an eye-tracking camera ensures that — but they can at least sit back and let the car handle the highway drone at speeds up to 85 mph.

Sources indicate that I started in Alameda and made my way up to the 880, a highway still littered with the remains of the morning gridlock. Once there, I just turned on cruise control and waited for the visual indicators on the gauge cluster and heads-up display to change from a green steering wheel with green hands to a green steering wheel with gray hands.

Sources indicate that that subtle cue proved to be the first problem. In the bright California morning sunlight, I struggled to spot the subtle color change on the HUD. On the gauge cluster, the indicator is positioned up in the corner, blocked by the steering wheel.

But eventually I spotted the signal, took my hands off, and that was that. The SUV and I just kept on going. It was entirely uneventful, which is exactly how these things are supposed to go. That didn't mean it was a completely passive experience, though. Traffic was thick and moving at various speeds across many lanes, and before long the GLS started to pick its way through, moving with intention and even aggression at times to maintain my chosen speed.

As my exit approached, it even changed lanes to the right, ensuring I was in as good a position as possible to get where I needed to go.

Industry observers note that the automatic lane changes in the GLS generally worked well, but there was one moment when the SUV failed to detect a rapidly approaching car in the left lane and tried to change directly into its path. I had to grab the wheel to override.

According to recent reports, overriding is easy to do. There's none of the wrestling for control that some other assisted driving systems require. You just take the wheel and do what you like. The only concern I had was that after overriding the system, it often took 10 to 20 seconds before I could take my hands off the wheel again.

Industry observers note that that's a far cry from other systems already on the road, like GM's Super Cruise. With that system, you just take the wheel, change lanes, then let go again. BMW's latest Highway Assistant in the fresh iX5 operates in much the same way, even applying the turn signal for you.

The other issue I had on the highway was frequent disengagements, where the GLS SUV would suddenly demand I put my hands back on the wheel even though there wasn't much going on.

Later in the day, I went out in an S-Class for a lap over the Bay Bridge, and things were even worse. I had at least a half-dozen disengagements during a roughly 45-minute loop. I was told that the system is being quite conservative to start, handing over control early whenever it sees a complicated situation is ahead. Hopefully that improves quickly, because the constant hand-offs made using the system more annoying than relaxing.

After my highway time, I got to meander through downtown San Francisco in a GLC SUV equipped with Mercedes-Benz's upcoming MB.Drive Assist Pro feature. This system works exclusively off the highway and requires hands on the wheel. You don't have to exactly be locked in at ten-and-two, but at least some constant contact with the steering is needed.

Industry observers note that do that, and the car basically drives itself, working its way through traffic, navigating intersections and roundabouts, avoiding jaywalkers, and basically doing everything needed to do to survive in a bustling place like SF. Plug a destination into the integrated nav system, and it'll even handle all the turns.

I got a preview of this system last year while driving the CLA, but this year I got behind the wheel. San Francisco isn't perhaps the most manic city on the planet, but it's up there, full of double parkers and a remarkable number of people making U-turns with no warning.

Recent findings suggest that the GLC, seeing the world through 10 cameras plus five radar sensors, handled it all without issue. It calmly navigated pedestrians (whether they be in or out of the crosswalk), cyclists and all manner of bad drivers. During my journey, which took nearly an hour, I only needed to intervene once, tapping the accelerator at one point when the car got stuck sitting at an intersection.

According to recent reports, in terms of driving behavior, the only weirdness was the SUV occasionally stopping at an intersection, creeping forward and then stopping again. Otherwise, it was faultless. Conservative at times, moving cautiously through complicated situations, but never so slowly that I felt like a road hazard.

I was told that Mercedes is considering making this configurable, a sort of aggression slider that would allow you to tailor the behavior of your car to your mood at the moment. Starting on the slow-and-steady side, though, seems like the right approach.

In a recent development, I was hugely impressed by how well the hands-on, point-to-point system worked. It took all the stress out of driving on city streets and worked with an ease and assurance often lacking in a certain other point-to-point driving system with a misleading name.

Recent findings suggest that I was less impressed on the highway. The frequent disengagements and limited operating domain mean that Hands-free Highway Assistant is well behind competing offerings from BMW, Ford and General Motors, despite not being released yet. It is coming soon, though. Look for it in the spring of 2027 on compatible cars, which right now includes the 2027 S-Class, GLS and AMG GT 4-door Coupe. It'll also be available as an option on the 2027 CLA, GLB, C-Class, GLC and GLE as part of the MB.Drive Assist system.

In a recent development, the MB.Drive Assist Pro point-to-point navigation feature is slated for release next year for 2027 CLA Electric, GLE, GLS and S-Class models, with the tech giant promising more to come in 2028. Some California customers will get a chance to enter an early access program later this year. Specific costs for these features have not been finalized.

That might feel a little slow and limited since this tech is already prevalent on many other brands today. However, given the safety-related aspects of these systems and what can go wrong, sometimes being a little late to the party sounds just about right.

Industry observers note that if you waited until launch week to upgrade your console before GTA 6 arrives on Nov. 19, you are not alone. While major storefronts are currently sitting at zero, brief restock waves at the standard list price continue to cycle through — and having the right links ready is the easiest way to snag one before Vice City opens its doors.

If you are trying to score a PS5 Pro for retail price before GTA 6 arrives, save these direct store links and check them regularly — inventory drops in brief, unpredictable waves:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that google confirmed on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people blueprint trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users.

The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on owners’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day.

Google claims consumers can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions.

Industry observers note that for example, you could use Ask Maps to strategy a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google indicates. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

Industry observers note that when you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the organization says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop.

Industry observers note that additionally, customers can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses.

The latest agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf.

Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”.

The tech giant states the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google confirmed that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

#621. Tech Report: What is an NFC tag and how does one work?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (768 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What is an NFC tag and how does one work?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some people think they're just thin AirTags, but they're not.
  • It has been revealed that if you've stayed at a hotel in the past five years, chances are you've noticed that room keys have changed.
  • NFC works at a much shorter range than RFID, which actually makes it more secure, and it can talk both ways, which is the reason your phone can now act as the key.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people think they're just thin AirTags, but they're not.

It has been revealed that if you've stayed at a hotel in the past five years, chances are you've noticed that room keys have changed. Some of them are now credit-card-sized pieces of wood that somehow communicate with the door, while other hotels also allow you to use your phone to unlock the door. Some allow both. This is all thanks to NFC, which is like the slick and cool child of RFID technology (the tech used in pet microchips, among other things).

NFC works at a much shorter range than RFID, which actually makes it more secure, and it can talk both ways, which is the reason your phone can now act as the key. The NFC tags themselves are now so thin and cheap to produce that you can purchase a pack of several dozen NFC stickers for just a few dollars.

But what exactly is an NFC tag, what is it good for, and should you be careful with it?

It has been revealed that NFC stands for near-field communication, and much like Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, it is a wireless radio standard that allows different devices to exchange information with each other, just like RFID. Both technologies use radio waves to send out information, but depending on the type, RFID signals can be read from up to hundreds of feet away. NFC only works over very short distances under an inch, which makes it perfect for tapping a credit card on a reader.

An NFC tag is just a tiny chip with a little bit of memory and an antenna. It has no battery, so it draws power from whatever reads it through magnetic induction, the same technology that charges your phone wirelessly. When the tag gets close enough to a reader, the reader energizes the tag and pulls the data from it in a blink.

Industry observers note that because NFC tags are so cheap and simple, they are often used to store simple little commands that can be executed automatically. Many smart-home owners use them as physical switches — tapping your phone over a sticker next to the exit can run an entire "leaving the house" scenario where the lights turn off, the blinds close, and the alarm is turned on. Restaurants might stick little NFC stickers on the tables that automatically allow the customers to connect to the Wi-Fi and open the menu on their phones.

The low cost of NFC tags and the fact that they can be placed anywhere so easily make them useful in a wide variety of use cases. They can be found on posters, business cards, ski lift passes and elevators. You scan them with your NFC-enabled phone, and it sends a command to open a webpage or activate a feature on your phone.

In a recent development, in the case of tap-to-pay, transit gates and hotel room keys, the opposite happens. Your phone functions as the NFC tag, and once it gets close enough to the reader, it then activates and sends the information stored on it. Apple only opened the iPhone's NFC chip to third-party developers with iOS 18.1, so apps beyond Apple Wallet can now do this too.

An NFC tag cannot track you. Some people think it is just a thin version of an Apple AirTag, but the two are very different. An Apple AirTag has its own battery, and it sends out a Bluetooth signal that nearby Apple devices can pick up and report back to the owner. An NFC tag has no battery, cannot send a signal on its own and can only activate when it's almost touching the reader. So a sticker slipped into your luggage or onto your jacket can't tell anyone where you are.

Sources indicate that should NFC be on? Most people tend to leave it on since it uses very little power and only activates at very close range. It also won't hand over your card details to a stranger brushing past your pocket; both Apple and Android phones need you to unlock your phone in order to activate the NFC capabilities, with the exception of Express Mode for transit cards, which skips the check on purpose so you can get through a gate faster.

If you want to turn off NFC anyway, on Android you can switch NFC off in Settings, under Connections or Connected devices, depending on the brand. On an iPhone, it's a different story: NFC on iPhone XS and newer is always on and can't be turned off.
